assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks opened a new regime of measurement: thousands of atoms interrogated at once in a magic-wavelength lattice, pushing fractional uncertainty to the 1e-18 level and beyond. This is a new instrument that lets us see things (gravitational redshift over millimetres, tests of constants) that were previously out of reach, and it feeds redefinition of the second. It is an original invention verified experimentally many times over.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice idea and made the first demonstrations with strontium; Jun Ye's group brought the clock to the highest accuracy and many-body regimes. These are the two natural decisive contributors within the credited list. Others (e.g. Lemonde, Takamoto) are not in the credited list and the allocation versus earlier ion-clock and frequency-comb prizes needs care.
assessment.maturity: Mature: multiple independent labs worldwide have confirmed the performance and clocks are comparing at the 1e-18 level. Recognition would be timely, with comb and ion-clock work already honoured in 2005 and 2012.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as sufficiently distinct from the earlier comb and single-ion clock prizes.
Allocation of credit to the original proposal versus the first experimental realization and the later accuracy record, which I cannot verify independently.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect form a clear discovery: a new class of electronic matter with protected edge states, predicted in theory and then seen in transport. Large conceptual impact, many follow-on materials, and the 2016 prize recognised topological phase transitions but not this specific discovery. The experimental confirmation is the key element for me.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical proposal (the Z2 invariant and quantum spin Hall effect in graphene). Molenkamp's group gave the original experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells in 2007, following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction, which is not in the supplied credit list. Hasan's 3D topological insulator ARPES work is a further important part but I would not make a four-way split.
assessment.maturity: Mature: quantum spin Hall edge transport and 3D topological insulators have been confirmed by many groups using transport and ARPES, with a stable interpretation.
uncertainties: The theory-experiment balance: BHZ prediction and the HgTe confirmation, and the 3D materials work by others, are partly outside the proposed set.
Whether graphene spin-orbit gap was too small for the Kane-Mele proposal to be realised, which complicates the credit narrative.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene created an entirely new tunable platform with flat bands, correlated insulators and superconductivity, which is a discovery driven by an experimental surprise and a precise theoretical prediction. Its impact on how people look for strongly correlated physics is already large, and microscopy and spectroscopy have been central to it.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the magic angle (2011); Jarillo-Herrero's group made the original 2018 observations of correlated insulators and superconductivity. Andrei's STM work on twisted graphene (van Hove singularities, flat bands) was an early independent experimental step. Fair credit among MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Andrei is possible, but the exclusion of Bistritzer from a three-person prize is a delicate point. I welcome nominating work by women where the record supports it, but the record must stand on its own.
assessment.maturity: Fairly young, around eight years; the experiment has been reproduced by many groups, but the nature of the superconductivity and the correlated states is still being debated.
uncertainties: Origin of the superconductivity is not settled, which raises the question of whether recognition is premature.
Credit among MacDonald, Bistritzer, Jarillo-Herrero, Andrei and others working on twisted graphene earlier is not fully resolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single defect spins in solids, notably the nitrogen-vacancy centre, created a room-temperature quantum sensor with nanoscale resolution that has real applications in materials and biology. For someone who images materials, a magnetometer on the nanometre scale that works under ambient conditions is a genuine new tool opening a door.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup's group first demonstrated optically detected magnetic resonance of a single NV centre (1997); Awschalom's group developed coherent control and spin manipulation in diamond and SiC defects; the nanoscale-sensing proposal and demonstrations were developed by Lukin, Walsworth and collaborators, so the credit is spread over more than three people and I cannot cleanly resolve it.
assessment.maturity: Quite mature with many groups replicating the results, and applications are developing; there is still ongoing development in sensing sensitivity and quantum networks. Timing is acceptable but the discovery is compound.
uncertainties: Compound discovery: single-defect detection, coherent control, and nanoscale sensing may need different recognition.
Walsworth, Degen and others not in the proposed triple also have strong claims.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: qPlus force sensing with CO-functionalized tips gave routine sub-molecular, bond-resolved imaging with atomic force microscopy, directly showing the structure of individual molecules and bond order. This is a step comparable in spirit to scanning tunnelling and atomic force microscopy, which have been honoured, and it is the kind of instrument development that lets us see what could not be seen before.
assessment.attribution: Giessibl invented the qPlus sensor; Gross, Meyer and colleagues at IBM Zurich demonstrated bond-resolved imaging with CO tips in 2009. The supplied credit seems to capture these decisive steps, though Mohn, Moll and Giessibl's own atomic-resolution work on silicon complicates the historical order.
assessment.maturity: Reasonably mature: widely used, reproduced and applied to on-surface chemistry. Impact on the broader field outside surface science is less than for other candidates.
uncertainties: Whether the physics discovery is deep enough compared with the technique and its chemistry applications.
Some further contributors (e.g. Mohn, Moll, Liljeroth) are not in the credited list.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance and then coherent MgO tunnel junctions gave large magnetoresistance and underpin read heads and magnetic random access memory. It is a clear experimental discovery with direct technological use, following on from the 2007 prize for giant magnetoresistance.
assessment.attribution: Moodera and Miyazaki independently reported room-temperature TMR in 1995. Large MgO TMR was reported by Yuasa et al. and by Parkin et al. in 2004, in parallel, following the Butler and Mathon theory. Selecting only three of Moodera, Miyazaki, Parkin and Yuasa is difficult, and I chose the two originators and one MgO pioneer, but this assignment is unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with decades of commercial use and many confirmations, and so timely or even late.
uncertainties: Four strong claimants for three places, and parallel work by Parkin and Yuasa makes the second step ambiguous.
The earlier GMR prize may make the committee view this as an incremental follow-up.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantized conductance in ballistic point contacts was a simple, original, verified experiment that showed conductance steps in units of 2e^2/h and became a foundation of mesoscopic physics and later quantum devices. It is clear and lasting, even if it is less in the public eye.
assessment.attribution: Two groups reported it independently and almost simultaneously in 1988: van Wees and colleagues in Delft and Wharam and colleagues, including Pepper, at Cambridge. The credited names capture both groups, so a prize is possible, though in a three-person limit the allocation between the two groups would need care.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, reproduced widely for over three decades. Recognition is perhaps late, and the committee may have viewed it as part of the quantum Hall and mesoscopic family already honoured.
uncertainties: Whether it is still relevant enough for a 2026 prize given the delay.
Lack of a theory or a direct measurement of a specific leader makes the three-person split less natural.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of X-ray and optical afterglows of gamma-ray bursts settled their cosmological origin and enabled redshift measurements, which turned a decades-old mystery into precision astrophysics. This is a discovery in the strict sense, resolved by an original observation.
assessment.attribution: Costa and Frontera's BeppoSAX team found the X-ray afterglow in 1997, and optical counterparts and redshifts followed from other groups, including Kulkarni's group. Names such as van Paradijs and Metzger are not in the credited list, so the allocation of credit is not complete and I cannot confirm who made the decisive contributions.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with more than 25 years of confirmation and a stable interpretation; the later link to gravitational-wave events adds further support.
uncertainties: Incomplete credited set: other observational teams made decisive optical and redshift measurements.
As an astrophysical observation rather than a laboratory experiment, I defer to colleagues on how it fits the physics criteria.
